title: Linux Reference
description: A quick reminder of the ideas and examples in the Linux lessons. Open the linked lesson when you need more help.

entries.name: Find your place
entries.summary: A terminal displays a shell, which reads commands. pwd prints the directory you are currently using.
notes: A terminal command acts in its current directory unless you give another path.

entries.name: List files
entries.summary: ls lists directory entries. The -a option includes names beginning with a dot, which are often hidden in normal views.
notes: A hidden file is not automatically private or secure.

entries.name: Create and enter a folder
entries.summary: mkdir creates a directory. cd changes the shell's current directory. Use a new name that does not replace existing work.
notes: A relative path starts from the current directory.

entries.name: Write and read a small file
entries.summary: printf writes text. A redirection sign sends that text into a file. cat prints a file's contents.
notes: A single > overwrites existing contents. Use it only on a practice file you intend to replace.

entries.name: Append a line
entries.summary: Two redirection signs append text to the end of a file. Earlier content stays in place.
notes: Do not confuse >> with >, which replaces the file contents.

entries.name: Copy a practice file
entries.summary: cp makes another copy of a file. Give a new destination name when you want to preserve both versions.
notes: cp may replace an existing destination; choose a fresh practice name.

entries.name: Search lines
entries.summary: grep prints lines that match a pattern. With -F it treats the pattern as fixed text rather than a special pattern language.
notes: A search is normally case-sensitive unless an option changes that rule.

entries.name: Count and sort
entries.summary: wc counts things such as lines. sort writes lines in order to its output. Piping connects one command's output to another.
notes: Sorting output does not rewrite the original file unless you explicitly write a result.

entries.name: Quote paths with spaces
entries.summary: Quotes keep several words together as one shell argument. This matters when a path contains spaces.
notes: Without quotes, the shell may treat a path as several arguments.

entries.name: Inspect permissions
entries.summary: Permissions describe who may read, write or execute a file. ls -l shows them along with other details.
notes: Do not grant every user write access just to make an error disappear.

entries.name: See running processes
entries.summary: A process is a running program. ps shows information about selected processes without stopping them.
notes: Do not stop a process you do not understand, especially on a shared computer.

entries.name: Write a tiny shell script
entries.summary: A script saves commands so you can run them again. This one only prints a greeting and the current path.

example.code:
printf '#!/bin/sh
printf "Hello, learner\n"
pwd
' > hello.sh
sh hello.sh

notes: Read a script before running it; a file extension does not make it safe.
